# 2 Samuel Chapter 11 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 179v–180r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_011_page_001.jpg, 2SA_011_page_002.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** In the spring of the year, at the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab and his servants with him and all Israel, and they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained in Jerusalem.

**2** One evening David arose from his bed and walked about on the roof of the king's house. From the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful.

**3** David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is this not Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"

**4** David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her — now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness — and she returned to her house.

**5** The woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."

**6** So David sent word to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.

**7** When Uriah came to him, David asked about the welfare of Joab, the welfare of the army, and the welfare of the war.

**8** Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah went out of the king's house, and a gift from the king followed him. **9** But Uriah lay down at the entrance of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.

**10** When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"

**11** Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camped in the open field. Shall I then go to my house to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing."

**12** David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.

**13** David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, and David made him drunk. But in the evening he went out to lie on his bed among the servants of his lord, and he did not go down to his house.

**14** In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.

**15** In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the fiercest fighting, then draw back from him, that he may be struck down and die."

**16** As Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew the strongest enemy warriors were. **17** The men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.

**18** Then Joab sent and reported to David all the events of the war.

**19** He instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling the king all the events of the war, **20** if the king's anger rises and he says to you, 'Why did you approach so near to the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall? **21** Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman throw an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you approach the wall?' — then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"

**22** The messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell. **23** The messenger said to David, "The men prevailed against us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate. **24** Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."

**25** David said to the messenger, "Thus you shall say to Joab: 'Do not let this matter trouble you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your assault against the city and overthrow it.' Encourage him."

**26** When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband.

**27** When the time of mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators recognize this as one of the most carefully crafted narratives in the Hebrew Bible. The consensus follows the chapter's distinctive style: flat, restrained prose that withholds moral commentary until the devastating final clause (v.27). The narrator's technique — reporting adultery, deception, and murder in the same understated tone used for military dispatches — is preserved by all three translators. Key structural elements are consistently identified: David's absence from battle (v.1), the parenthetical about purification (v.4), Uriah's ironic oath (v.11), the letter carried by the condemned man (v.14-15), David's callous proverb (v.25), and the divine verdict (v.27).

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "at the turn of the year" vs. "in the spring"
- **EMET:** "at-[the]-turn of-the-year [litshuvat ha-shanah]"
- **LOGOS:** "In the spring of the year"
- **PNEUMA:** "In the spring"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "In the spring of the year" — *litshuvat ha-shanah* literally means "at the return of the year" but idiomatically refers to spring, the campaigning season. LOGOS captures both the temporal idiom and its military significance.

### V.1 — "sitting" vs. "remained" vs. "stayed behind"
- **EMET:** "David [was]-sitting [yoshev]"
- **LOGOS:** "David remained"
- **PNEUMA:** "David stayed behind"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "David remained" — *yoshev* (sitting/dwelling) is neutral in EMET but gains moral weight from context. LOGOS's "remained" is neutral like the Hebrew. PNEUMA's "stayed behind" adds a hint of judgment not yet present in the text.

### V.2 — "good of appearance" vs. "very beautiful" vs. "strikingly beautiful"
- **EMET:** "good of-appearance [tovat mar'eh] exceedingly"
- **LOGOS:** "very beautiful"
- **PNEUMA:** "strikingly beautiful"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "very beautiful" — *tovat mar'eh me'od* = "very good of appearance." LOGOS's translation is standard and accurate. PNEUMA's "strikingly" adds emphasis beyond the Hebrew.

### V.4 — purification clause placement and wording
- **EMET:** "and-she [was]-purifying-herself [mitqaddeshet] from-her-uncleanness [tum'atah]"
- **LOGOS:** "now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness"
- **PNEUMA:** "She had just completed her ritual purification after her monthly period"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness" — LOGOS preserves the parenthetical nature of the clause and the key terms (*mitqaddeshet*, *tum'ah*). PNEUMA's expansion ("monthly period," "just completed") adds interpretation.

### V.8 — "wash your feet" (euphemism question)
- **EMET:** "wash your-feet" (literal)
- **LOGOS:** "wash your feet"
- **PNEUMA:** "wash your feet"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** All agree on the literal rendering. The phrase *rechats raglekha* may be a euphemism for marital intimacy (cf. the use of "feet" as euphemism elsewhere in Hebrew), or simply hospitality language. The ambiguity is preserved.

### V.11 — "by your life and by the life of your soul" vs. "I swear on your very life"
- **EMET:** "By-your-life [chayyekha] and-by-[the]-life of-your-soul [chey nafshekha]"
- **LOGOS:** "As you live, and as your soul lives"
- **PNEUMA:** "As surely as you live — I swear on your very life"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "As you live, and as your soul lives" — LOGOS preserves the double oath formula. PNEUMA collapses the two clauses into one and adds "I swear," which is interpretive.

### V.15 — "set" vs. "put" vs. "place"
- **EMET:** "Set [havu] Uriyah"
- **LOGOS:** "Set Uriah"
- **PNEUMA:** "Put Uriah at the front"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Set Uriah in the forefront" — *havu* is an imperative meaning "give/set/place." "Set" (EMET/LOGOS) is more precise than PNEUMA's "put."

### V.25 — "be evil in your eyes" vs. "trouble you" vs. "upset you"
- **EMET:** "Do-not let-this-thing be-evil in-your-eyes"
- **LOGOS:** "Do not let this matter trouble you"
- **PNEUMA:** "Don't let this upset you"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Do not let this matter trouble you" — the Hebrew *al-yera be-einekha* literally means "let it not be evil in your eyes." LOGOS's "trouble" captures the sense while EMET's literalism and PNEUMA's casualness are both less suitable for the consensus.

### V.25 — "the sword devours now one and now another" vs. "cuts down one man as easily as another"
- **EMET:** "thus and-thus the-sword devours [tokhal]"
- **LOGOS:** "the sword devours now one and now another"
- **PNEUMA:** "the sword cuts down one man as easily as another"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the sword devours now one and now another" — LOGOS preserves the personification (*tokhal* = devours) and the Hebrew idiom *kazeh ve-kazeh* (now this one, now that one). PNEUMA's "cuts down" loses the devouring metaphor.

### V.26 — "wife of Uriah" vs. "Uriah's wife"
- **EMET:** "[the]-wife of-Uriyah"
- **LOGOS:** "the wife of Uriah"
- **PNEUMA:** "Uriah's wife"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the wife of Uriah" — the narrator deliberately avoids Bathsheba's name in this verse, referring to her only as "the wife of Uriah." This is not accidental; it reinforces that she belongs to Uriah. Both EMET and LOGOS preserve this.

### V.27 — "was evil in the eyes of the LORD" vs. "was evil in the eyes of YHWH"
- **EMET:** "was-evil [vayera] in-[the]-eyes of-YHWH"
- **LOGOS:** "was evil in the eyes of the LORD"
- **PNEUMA:** "was evil in the eyes of the LORD"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** All three agree on the substance. "The LORD" follows project convention for YHWH.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
